title: Ewe Emoji 🐑 Meaning: Sheep, Lambs and the Good Shepherd
description: 🐑, the ewe emoji, is the sheep: counting sheep, wool, following the crowd, the Good Shepherd and the Lamb of God. See its everyday and Christian meanings.
summary: The 🐑 ewe emoji shows a fluffy white sheep. Unicode calls it a ewe, a female sheep, but people use it for any sheep or lamb: counting sheep to fall asleep, wool and knitting, farm life, following the crowd, and Christian images of the Good Shepherd, the shepherds at Bethlehem, and the Lamb of God.
meaning: There is no separate lamb emoji, so 🐑 does all the sheep work. Literal uses include farms, petting zoos, spring lambing season, and wool, which makes it popular with knitters and spinners alongside 🧶. Insomniacs post it for counting sheep, and "🐑🐑🐑 💤" is a quick way to say you are trying to sleep. Visitors to New Zealand, Wales, and Ireland use it in travel captions about roads blocked by flocks.

Figuratively, a sheep follows the crowd. Calling people sheep, or "sheeple," accuses them of going along with something without thinking, so 🐑 in an argument is often an insult. In a gentler sense, it can mean meek or shy, and a black sheep is the family member who does not fit in, though there is no black sheep emoji.

Christian imagery is full of sheep. Jesus calls himself the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for his sheep, and the parable of the lost sheep describes leaving the ninety-nine to find the one. Christ is called the Lamb of God, "Agnus Dei," words said at every Catholic Mass before Communion. Pastors are shepherds of a flock, and the word pastor itself comes from the Latin for shepherd.

At Christmas, 🐑 joins the nativity scene with the shepherds who were keeping watch over their flocks when the angels appeared. At Easter, the lamb represents the risen Christ, and lamb is a traditional Easter meal in many countries. In Islam, sheep are commonly sacrificed for Eid al-Adha, where 🐑 and 🐏 both appear in greetings.

contexts.label: In church and holiday posts
contexts.body: Parishes use 🐑 for Good Shepherd Sunday, Easter, and children's ministry lessons about the lost sheep. At Christmas it fills out nativity scenes beside 🐂, 🫏, and 👶, standing for the shepherds' flocks. Lamb-themed Easter treats, like butter lambs and lamb cakes, are posted with it as well.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: Most everyday uses are sleepy or cute. "Counting 🐑" means insomnia; a picture of a fluffy dog might get "looks like a sheep 🐑." In arguments, it means the other person is a follower. The tone depends on whether it arrives with 💤 or with an eye roll.

contexts.label: In knitting and farming
contexts.body: Fiber artists use 🐑 for wool sources, yarn hauls, and fleece processing, often with 🧶. Farmers and homesteaders use it for lambing updates in spring, shearing day, and county fair livestock shows. Here it is entirely literal and usually affectionate, a little mascot for the flock.

confusedWith.difference: 🐏 is a male sheep with curled horns, used for strength, Aries, and the Los Angeles Rams. 🐑 is a hornless, woolly ewe and suits lambs, gentleness, and wool.
🐐 is a goat with a beard and straight horns, and in slang means GOAT, greatest of all time. 🐑 has nothing to do with that and simply means sheep.

avoid: Do not call people 🐑 in a serious disagreement unless you mean to insult them as mindless followers.
Avoid using it for the GOAT compliment; that is 🐐, and mixing them up changes the meaning.
design: A whole sheep in side view with a puffy white fleece, a small face peeking out at one end, and thin legs. Most designs give it a fluffy, cloud-like body and no horns, which is what separates it from 🐏. Styles vary slightly in how cartoonish the fleece is but are consistent across platforms.

faqs.a: No. 🐑 is used for lambs, ewes, and sheep in general. For Easter posts and references to the Lamb of God, 🐑 is the standard choice, sometimes paired with ✝️ or 🕊️.

faqs.q: What does 🐑 mean in an argument?
faqs.a: It usually means "you're a sheep": someone who follows the crowd or believes what they are told without questioning it. It is meant as an insult in that context.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 🐑 and 🐏?
faqs.a: 🐑 is a ewe, a female sheep without horns. 🐏 is a ram, a male sheep with curled horns. People use 🐑 for sheep in general and 🐏 for strength, Aries, or the Rams.

faqs.q: Why are sheep in the nativity scene?
faqs.a: In the Gospel of Luke, shepherds were watching their flocks at night near Bethlehem when angels announced the birth of Jesus. Their sheep became part of crib scenes and Christmas pageants.
